summary: Specifies a new NAT traversal mode for the Host Identity Protocol, based on ICE methodology and UDP encapsulation. Unlike earlier modes, it uses HIP messages instead of ICE for all the NAT traversal procedures.

eli5.summary: Two computers behind home routers that block unexpected visitors use this to find a way to talk directly.

questions: what is a hip data relay server
subtitle: A way for two hosts using the Host Identity Protocol to find a direct path through NATs, using HIP's own messages instead of STUN and TURN.

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol runs directly on IP, but NATs and firewalls often let only UDP or TCP through. The earlier ICE-based answer, Legacy ICE-HIP, needs a full ICE/STUN/TURN stack and performs poorly for kernel-space implementations.
tldr.mechanism: Native ICE-HIP wraps HIP control and ESP packets in UDP, registers hosts with relay servers, swaps candidate addresses inside the HIP base exchange, and then tests address pairs with HIP UPDATE packets until one pair is nominated.
tldr.outcome: Hosts get a UDP tunnel directly between NATs or through a Data Relay Server, with keepalives and mobility handled in the same HIP messages. The RFC is Experimental.

today: RFC 9028 is an Experimental RFC from July 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It offers an alternative to Legacy ICE-HIP (RFC 5770) and builds on HIPv2 (RFC 7401).

sections.title: Why a Native Mode Is Needed
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) runs directly on top of IPv4 or IPv6, but many middleboxes such as NATs and firewalls often allow only UDP or TCP traffic to pass. NATs also usually require the host behind them to create forwarding state before outside hosts can contact it.

An earlier specification, RFC 5770 (called Legacy ICE-HIP), combines HIP with the ICE protocol, using STUN and TURN messages. The authors say HIP's close integration with kernel-space IPsec makes that route incur unacceptable performance drawbacks for kernel-space implementations, and that integrating a full ICE/STUN/TURN stack takes considerable effort and code.

Native ICE-HIP keeps the ICE methodology but uses the HIP message format for connectivity checks, keepalives and data relaying. It is based on HIPv2, whereas the legacy specification is based on HIPv1, and it also describes mobility handling in the context of NAT traversal, which Legacy ICE-HIP lacks.
sections.eli5: The old way needed a whole extra toolbox. The new way reuses the tools HIP already has.

sections.title: Relays, Candidates and the Overall Flow
sections.content:
Two kinds of relay appear. A Control Relay Server forwards HIP control packets between the Initiator and the Responder, replacing HIP Rendezvous Servers for hosts in private address realms. A Data Relay Server is new in this document; it forwards data-plane packets such as ESP and does a job similar to a TURN server.

The flow is: both hosts register with a relay and gather address candidates (host, server-reflexive and relayed). The base exchange then runs inside UDP datagrams through the Responder's Control Relay Server, and each host learns the peer's candidates from the HIP offer and answer carried in it. After that, connectivity checks look for a better path, ideally without a Data Relay Server. When one is found, the hosts have a UDP tunnel, kept alive with NAT keepalives.

The Initiator is always the controlling host, which nominates the candidate pair, and the Responder is always the controlled host.
sections.eli5: Helpers outside pass the first notes. Then the two kids try different paths to each other until one works, and keep it open by waving every so often.

sections.title: Registration and Negotiation
sections.content:
Registration follows the HIP registration extensions. A host registers for control relaying with the Registration Type RELAY_UDP_HIP, and for UDP-encapsulated ESP relaying with RELAY_UDP_ESP (value 3). The relay returns the host's address as it sees it in a REG_FROM parameter (a server-reflexive candidate) and, for data relaying, the allocated port in RELAYED_ADDRESS. It is RECOMMENDED that relays listen on UDP port 10500 and that clients choose a source port from 49152-65535.

The hosts negotiate in the base exchange with a non-critical NAT_TRAVERSAL_MODE parameter. This document adds the mode ICE-HIP-UDP (value 3). Locators go in a LOCATOR_SET parameter inside an ENCRYPTED parameter: the Initiator's in I2 is the HIP offer, the Responder's in R2 is the answer.

Hosts also agree on a pacing value Ta for connectivity checks with a TRANSACTION_PACING parameter. The higher offered value is used, the default is 50 ms and values below 5 ms MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: First you sign in with the helper and say which tricks you know. Then you agree on how quickly to knock, so you do not overwhelm the doors.

sections.title: Connectivity Checks and Nomination
sections.content:
Checks are HIP UPDATE packets sent over UDP. Each carries a SEQ and an ECHO_REQUEST_SIGNED, plus a CANDIDATE_PRIORITY, and is answered with ACK, ECHO_RESPONSE_SIGNED and a MAPPED_ADDRESS that reveals the sender's address as seen by the peer. All checks MUST be protected with HIP_HMAC and signatures, and the HIT pair serves as the credentials instead of ICE's username and password fragments.

Checks go out in priority order, paced by Ta. The retransmission timeout is MAX (1000 ms, Ta * (Num-Waiting + Num-In-Progress)), and it is RECOMMENDED to cap the checks at 100 per host association.

To finish, the controlling host repeats a check on the best working pair with a NOMINATE parameter. The controlled host answers with its own, and the controlling host confirms. Then both can create IPsec security associations and send ESP over UDP. If every check fails, hosts MUST NOT send ESP to each other, but MAY keep using HIP over the base exchange locators.
sections.eli5: Each side knocks on every possible door, best first. When one works, the leader says this is the one, the other agrees, and they start talking.

sections.title: Keepalives, Mobility and Closing
sections.content:
To keep NAT state from expiring, hosts MUST send keepalives every 15 seconds, and a smaller interval MUST NOT be used. The recommended form is a HIP NOTIFY packet of type NAT_KEEPALIVE (16385) with empty data, which may be left out if other traffic has flowed over the tunnel.

When a host moves, it first sends its new locators to its relays, waiting by default two minutes for replies. It then runs an UPDATE handover with each peer and re-tests connectivity. This offers the same function as ICE restart, and only simple mobility is covered; multihoming is left to later specifications.

Closing uses the usual CLOSE and CLOSE_ACK exchange over the UDP tunnel. A sender should try the direct path first, and after some retransmissions MUST use the recipient's Control Relay Server if one exists.
sections.eli5: Every so often you wave to keep the door from locking. If you move house, you tell the helper and your friend your new address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The control plane and Control Relay Server are essentially as in Legacy ICE-HIP, so those security considerations are repeated. New ones concern the Data Relay Server and the connectivity checks.

A Data Relay Server SHOULD NOT reuse port numbers across clients. If it did, a stateful firewall would see all clients at one address and might let through packets from hosts that should not be allowed. A malicious host could also hand its peer a bogus candidate list so that the peer floods a victim with checks; the cap on the number of checks limits this.

The RFC also has sections on privacy, opportunistic mode, replay protection of the base exchange via a relay, attacks on candidate gathering, and cross-protocol attacks.
sections.eli5: Helpers must not give two kids the same window, and nobody should be tricked into knocking on a stranger's door a thousand times.
